To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the immune system is able to control leukemic cells, including LSCs, by activating leukemia-specific CD8+ and CD4+ T cells.
the BM microenvironment is a key regulator of hematopoiesis and leukemia.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of novel mechanisms that contribute to the regulation of normal and malignant hematopoiesis by the immune system.
the interaction of immune and hematopoietic cells in the BM microenvironment and how this interaction affects the function and survival of normal and malignant HSCs.
understanding the mechanisms that control HSCs and leukemic stem cell function in the context of the immune system and to exploit this knowledge for the development of novel therapies for leukemia.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the BM microenvironment is a complex and dynamic system that is able to regulate both normal and malignant HSCs in a highly flexible manner, depending on the actual needs and the current situation of the organism.
the immune system has a complex and dual role in regulating HSCs and leukemic stem/progenitor cells.
the immune system is a double-edged sword in regulating normal and leukemic hematopoiesis.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the immune system is able to control leukemic cells and LSCs but the actual interaction of LSCs with immune cells remains to be defined and needs to be further investigated.
the immune system is a double-edged sword for the regulation of HSCs.
the immune system is not only able to control LSCs but also to promote leukemia progression.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the BM niche and the immune system are tightly interwoven and that immune cells are not only able to eliminate leukemia cells, but also to support LSCs and promote leukemogenesis.
immune cells may contribute to the maintenance and progression of leukemia and that the immune system is not only a potential therapy for leukemia but may also be part of the disease.
the immune system is an important player in the regulation of LSCs and may be a promising target for future leukemia therapy.
